title: Affordable Care Act (ACA)
summary: The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (P.L. 111-148), signed March 23, 2010 and amended a week later by the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 (P.L. 111-152). Created the health insurance Marketplaces with income-based premium tax credits, extended Medicaid to adults with incomes up to 138% of the federal poverty level (optional for states after NFIB v. Sebelius, 2012), and required guaranteed issue, community rating, essential health benefits and dependent coverage to age 26. Its main coverage provisions took effect January 1, 2014. The individual-mandate penalty has been $0 since 2019 under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, and the Supreme Court left the law standing in NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), King v. Burwell (2015) and California v. Texas (2021).
relevance_note: The statute behind most of today's non-employer private coverage and the Medicaid expansion. The dashboard's 2023 spending base already includes it; the rows below track the 2025-2026 changes to its subsidies and enrollment rules.
model_link_note: Already inside the 2023 spending base the model starts from; no parameter prices the statute itself.

title: No Surprises Act
summary: Enacted as Title I of Division BB of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 (P.L. 116-260), signed December 27, 2020; most provisions apply to plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2022. Bars surprise balance billing for emergency services, for non-emergency care from out-of-network clinicians at in-network facilities, and for air ambulance services, limiting the patient's cost sharing to in-network amounts. Payment disputes between plans and out-of-network providers go to a federal independent dispute resolution process, and uninsured or self-pay patients are entitled to a good-faith cost estimate.
relevance_note: Current federal floor on surprise billing. The plan's provider domain lists it among the protections retained while legacy private coverage runs in parallel.
model_link_note: A billing protection inside the 2023 base. With no charge at the point of care, the bills it governs do not arise, and no parameter prices it.

title: Inflation Reduction Act - Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program (First Cycle, IPAY 2026)
summary: Under IRA Section 11001 (P.L. 117-169), CMS negotiated Medicare Part D "maximum fair prices" for the first 10 selected drugs (Eliquis, Jardiance, Xarelto, Januvia, Farxiga, Entresto, Enbrel, Imbruvica, Stelara, NovoLog/Fiasp). Negotiated prices took effect January 1, 2026, with CMS estimating about 22% lower net Medicare spending on these drugs versus 2023 baseline prices.
relevance_note: First real-world application of Medicare's new drug price negotiation authority; sets the template for future negotiation cycles.
model_link_note: Negotiated Medicare prices from 2026 lower the status-quo net prices the national purchasing cut is measured from (2023), so part of the modelled cut on these drugs is realized under current law. Not yet estimated in the comparator.

title: Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program - Second Cycle (IPAY 2027, 15 Drugs)
summary: CMS reached agreement with manufacturers on negotiated maximum fair prices for 15 additional Part D drugs, including the Ozempic/semaglutide family, covering about 5.3 million beneficiaries and $42.5 billion in 2024 Part D spending. Prices are finalized but do not take effect until January 1, 2027.
relevance_note: Confirms the negotiation program is scaling on schedule under the IRA; second data point for tracking realized savings.
model_link_note: Fifteen more negotiated prices from 2027 lower the same status-quo comparator further. Not yet estimated.

title: IRA Medicare Part D Benefit Redesign - $2,000 Annual Out-of-Pocket Cap
summary: IRA Section 11202 restructured the Part D benefit into a three-phase design (deductible, initial coverage, catastrophic), eliminated the coverage-gap "donut hole," and capped enrollee out-of-pocket drug costs at $2,000/year, indexed annually ($2,100 for CY2026). Enrollees may also spread costs in equal monthly installments via the Medicare Prescription Payment Plan.
relevance_note: Already-realized consumer affordability change, distinct from and often conflated with the negotiation program.
model_link_note: Lowers status-quo Part D out-of-pocket costs from 2025; the model's base year predates it and the plan removes point-of-care costs at any level, so no parameter moves.

title: Executive Order: Delivering Most-Favored-Nation Prescription Drug Pricing to American Patients
summary: Directs HHS/CMS to set most-favored-nation price targets for manufacturers and threatens rulemaking, drug importation waivers, and antitrust enforcement if voluntary compliance falls short. Has since produced individual manufacturer pricing agreements (starting September 2025) and proposed CMS payment models (GLOBE for Part B, GUARD for Part D) rather than one binding rule.
relevance_note: Primary driver of 2025-2026 federal drug-pricing activity; underlying framework for the manufacturer deals and forthcoming GLOBE/GUARD models.
model_link_note: Voluntary manufacturer agreements and proposed payment models; no binding price change yet exists to put in a comparator. If one is finalized, it belongs with drugPriceCut.

title: Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 - PBM Reform Provisions (H.R. 7148)
summary: Signed into law February 3, 2026 (P.L. 119-75). Section 6702 amends ERISA section 408(b)(2): for plan years beginning 30 months after enactment (on or after August 3, 2028, so January 1, 2029, for calendar-year plans), a contract for pharmacy benefit management services entered into, renewed or extended from then on is not reasonable, and so not exempt from ERISA's prohibited-transaction rules, unless the PBM remits 100 percent of the rebates, fees, alternative discounts and other remuneration it receives from manufacturers, wholesalers, rebate aggregators, affiliated group purchasing organizations and other applicable entities to the plan (or to the insurer on the plan's behalf), quarterly; a contract in force keeps its terms until it is renewed or extended. Section 6701 requires PBMs, on the same schedule, to report to group health plans at least every six months (quarterly at the plan's request), including claim by claim what the plan paid against what the pharmacy was paid. The law also shifts Medicare Part D PBM compensation to flat bona-fide service fees effective January 1, 2028 (section 6224, plan years beginning on or after that date); and requires the contract terms a Part D plan offers any willing pharmacy to be reasonable and relevant, effective January 1, 2029 (section 6223).
relevance_note: First major enacted federal PBM transparency and delinking law; a structural change to drug-pricing intermediaries.
model_link_note: Rebate pass-through to employer plans and Part D delinking lower what plans pay net of rebates, part of the comparator the national purchasing cut is measured from. Not yet estimated. The Workforce chapter's PBM slice, a scenario of the PBM functions the plan replaces and not a model parameter, is unaffected: the law changes how PBMs are paid and what they disclose, not which functions exist.

title: American Hospital Association v. Kennedy - 340B Rebate Model Pilot Vacated
summary: The U.S. District Court for the District of Maine preliminarily enjoined (December 29, 2025) and then vacated and remanded to HRSA (February 10, 2026) the agency's 340B Rebate Model Pilot Program, which would have let manufacturers issue 340B discounts as after-the-fact rebates instead of upfront ceiling-price discounts. HRSA must restart via notice-and-comment to pursue a rebate model.
relevance_note: Preserved the upfront-discount 340B structure. HRSA has since issued a revised pilot, set to begin January 1, 2027 and challenged in a new suit; it has its own row.
model_link_note: Keeps the 340B upfront discount as it was in the base year; nothing in the model changes.

title: Hospital Price Transparency Rule (45 CFR Part 180) - 2024 Standardization Amendments
summary: Finalized November 2023, effective January 1, 2024. Requires hospitals to post standard charges, including negotiated rates, cash prices, and payer-specific amounts, in a CMS-standardized machine-readable file format, with a homepage footer link and a required .txt file for automated discovery. Builds on the original 2019 hospital price transparency rule, effective 2021.
relevance_note: Core federal price-transparency mandate for hospitals; baseline against which later enforcement and format updates should be tracked.
model_link_note: A disclosure rule; no parameter depends on hospital price posting.

title: CY 2026 OPPS/ASC Final Rule - Hospital Price Transparency Enforcement & Data Updates
summary: Published November 25, 2025 as part of the CY2026 OPPS/ASC final rule. Requires hospitals to report a Type 2 NPI, replaces the "Estimated Allowed Amount" field with four allowed-amount data points (median, 10th/90th percentile, count), and revises civil monetary penalty procedures, including a 35% CMP reduction for hospitals that waive an ALJ hearing. Effective January 1, 2026; CMS delayed enforcement to April 1, 2026, which has now passed.
relevance_note: Most recent enforcement and format tightening of the hospital price transparency regime; likely source of near-term compliance news.
model_link_note: A disclosure and enforcement rule; no parameter depends on it.

title: Transparency in Coverage Final Rule (CMS-9915-F)
summary: Requires most group health plans and issuers to publicly post machine-readable files disclosing in-network negotiated rates and historical out-of-network allowed amounts, plus (from 2023) an internet self-service price comparison tool for consumers. In-network/out-of-network machine-readable files became required July 1, 2022. The companion prescription-drug pricing file remains deferred under enforcement discretion; the October 6, 2026 final rule (CMS-9882-F) says the Departments plan to begin working to implement it in short order.
relevance_note: Payer-side counterpart to the hospital price transparency rule. The December 2025 proposal was finalized October 6, 2026 (CMS-9882-F) and has its own row.
model_link_note: A disclosure rule for private plans; no parameter depends on it.

title: One Big Beautiful Bill Act - ACA Marketplace & Individual Market Provisions (P.L. 119-21)
summary: Signed July 4, 2025. Ends Marketplace subsidy eligibility for lawfully present immigrants in their first five years in the U.S. (effective January 1, 2026), terminates continuous income-based special enrollment periods, removes premium tax credit repayment caps, and shortens open enrollment windows. Enacted through budget reconciliation alongside sweeping Medicaid changes in the same law.
relevance_note: Largest enacted change to ACA marketplace eligibility and enrollment rules since the ACA itself; a direct input for coverage-simulation baselines.
model_link_note: Narrows Marketplace subsidy eligibility and enrollment from 2026, raising the uninsured count after the 2024 figure the demand parameters use, and lowering projected federal spending after the 2025 projections the baseline growth uses.

title: Expiration of ACA Enhanced Premium Tax Credits (ARPA/IRA Sunset)
summary: The enhanced premium tax credits first enacted by the American Rescue Plan Act (2021) and extended through 2025 by the Inflation Reduction Act (2022) lapsed automatically at the start of 2026 after a Senate extension bill (S.3385) failed to reach 60 votes. The House passed a three-year extension on January 8, 2026 (230-196) after a discharge petition; no Senate passage was found as of October 10, 2026. Marketplace enrollees now face pre-2021 subsidy formulas.
relevance_note: Major, already-effective affordability shock to ACA marketplace consumers; central input for coverage and uninsured-rate modeling.
model_link_note: Raises the uninsured count after the 2024 figure the demand parameters use. The baseline growth projections already assumed the expiry, which was current law when they were made.

title: One Big Beautiful Bill Act - Medicaid Provisions (P.L. 119-21)
summary: Signed July 4, 2025. Establishes Medicaid community engagement (work) requirements for expansion adults ages 19-64, mandates more frequent eligibility redeterminations, tightens provider-tax and state-directed-payment financing tools, and narrows immigration-status eligibility. Its provisions take effect on a staggered schedule: the limit on state-directed payments took effect July 4, 2025, for managed-care rating periods beginning on or after that date; CMS's rule implementing the law's closing of a provider-tax loophole took effect April 3, 2026; the cap on new or increased provider taxes, the narrower immigration-status eligibility, and the limit of emergency Medicaid for people otherwise eligible as expansion adults to the regular federal match took effect October 1, 2026; the work requirement applies from January 1, 2027; the expansion-state provider-tax phase-down begins in fiscal year 2028.
relevance_note: Largest enacted change to Medicaid financing and eligibility rules in over a decade; primary statutory driver of projected Medicaid coverage losses.
model_link_note: Cuts federal Medicaid financing and adds work requirements and more frequent redeterminations; projected to raise the uninsured count after the 2024 figure and to lower spending below the June 2025 projections, which predate it.

title: CMS Interim Final Rule - Medicaid Community Engagement (Work) Requirement (CMS-2454-IFC)
summary: Published June 3, 2026 (91 FR 33348) and in force since July 31, 2026. Implements OBBBA's Medicaid work-requirement provision under Social Security Act section 1902(xx). Requires non-pregnant adults ages 19-64 in the Medicaid adult group (or applicable Section 1115 demonstrations) to complete 80 hours/month of work, education, training, or community service, or meet an earnings-based equivalent, unless exempt (pregnancy, disability, medical frailty, caregiving, short-term hardship). States must implement by January 1, 2027. A multistate challenge to the rule's narrowing of the medically frail exemption (Massachusetts v. Oz, D. Mass.) is pending; the court denied a preliminary injunction on July 29, 2026, without prejudice.
relevance_note: Operational implementing regulation states must follow; defines the exemption categories and compliance mechanics needed to model coverage-loss scenarios.
model_link_note: Puts the Medicaid work requirement into operation from January 2027; the same three parameters as the provision it implements.

title: CY 2026 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule (CMS-1832-F)
summary: Published November 5, 2025, effective January 1, 2026. Implements MACRA's statutorily required separate conversion factors for Advanced Alternative Payment Model (APM) participants versus non-APM clinicians, keeps the MIPS performance threshold at 75 points through the 2028 performance period, and launches the mandatory Ambulatory Specialty Model, a MIPS Value Pathway-based program covering heart failure and low back pain with payment adjustments that widen over time.
relevance_note: Core annual determinant of Medicare physician payment and the newest mandatory value-based/site-neutral-style payment model.
model_link_note: An annual payment update inside status-quo spending growth; the payment factor is set against average rates, not one year's schedule.

title: FDA Final Guidance - Predetermined Change Control Plans for AI-Enabled Device Software Functions
summary: Establishes FDA's recommended framework letting manufacturers pre-specify planned AI/ML modifications in a marketing submission (a Predetermined Change Control Plan), so later approved algorithm updates do not require new 510(k), De Novo, or PMA submissions. Applies to all AI-enabled device software functions, not only machine-learning-based ones.
relevance_note: Foundational current framework for how adaptive, learning-capable AI medical devices are regulated after initial clearance.
model_link_note: Device-review guidance; no parameter depends on it.

title: FDA Final Guidance - Cybersecurity in Medical Devices (QMSR-Aligned)
summary: Issued February 3, 2026, superseding the June 2025 version. Updates premarket cybersecurity submission recommendations (secure product development framework, threat modeling, software bill of materials, penetration testing) to align with the new Quality Management System Regulation, which replaced the old Quality System Regulation (21 CFR 820) with ISO 13485:2016 effective February 2, 2026. Core technical expectations are unchanged from 2025.
relevance_note: Governs cybersecurity documentation for all connected and software-driven medical devices, an increasing share of which incorporate AI.
model_link_note: Device-review guidance; no parameter depends on it.

title: ASTP/ONC HTI-4 Final Rule - E-Prescribing, Real-Time Prescription Benefit & Electronic Prior Authorization
summary: Finalizes new and updated health IT certification criteria for electronic prior authorization, electronic prescribing, and real-time prescription benefit information, plus related API standards, as part of the FY2026 CMS Hospital Inpatient Prospective Payment System final rule (CMS-1833-F). Effective October 1, 2025.
relevance_note: Latest binding interoperability and certification standard shaping EHR-to-payer data exchange infrastructure.
model_link_note: Health IT certification standards; the information-mesh cost parameters are priced from enterprise benchmarks, not from this rule.

title: ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions & Withdrawal of HTI-2 Patient Engagement/Public Health Interoperability Rule
summary: Published December 29, 2025. Formally withdraws the pending HTI-2 "Patient Engagement, Information Sharing, and Public Health Interoperability" proposed rule from the prior administration and finalizes a companion deregulatory rule narrowing certain health IT certification and information-blocking provisions.
relevance_note: Marks a policy reversal in federal health IT regulation; important for tracking regulatory direction and the resulting compliance uncertainty ASTP/ONC's later HTI-5 proposal is meant to address.
model_link_note: Withdraws a proposed interoperability rule; no parameter assumed it.

title: Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act - 2024 Final Rule (Non-Enforcement Status)
summary: The 2024 MHPAEA final rule, requiring group health plans to show "meaningful benefits" for mental health/substance use disorder care and to conduct comparative analyses of nonquantitative treatment limitations, was challenged by the ERISA Industry Committee in January 2025 in D.D.C. Following a May 12, 2025 litigation stay, DOL, HHS, and Treasury announced on May 15, 2025 that they will not enforce the 2024 rule pending the litigation's outcome, plus an additional 18 months after any final decision. In a March 30, 2026 status report the Departments said they would no longer defend the rule and intend to propose replacement rules by the end of 2026; the case remains on hold.
relevance_note: The rule remains technically "final" but is functionally non-operative - an important distinction for any parity-compliance modeling.
model_link_note: Not enforced pending litigation; the behavioral-health expansion is priced from unmet need, not from parity enforcement.

title: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline - FY2026 Administrator Funding Award
summary: SAMHSA awarded $255 million to Vibrant Emotional Health to continue administering the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline for FY2026, following a roughly $231 million FY2026 funding opportunity announcement. The award followed a contested administration budget proposal that would have eliminated specialized LGBTQ+ youth crisis-service funding after September 30, 2025.
relevance_note: 988 is the primary federal behavioral-health crisis infrastructure; funding continuity directly affects crisis-system capacity assumptions.
model_link_note: Continues existing crisis-line funding inside the status quo; no parameter moves.

title: Idaho v. United States / Moyle v. United States - EMTALA Emergency Abortion Case Dismissed
summary: The Supreme Court dismissed its June 2024 grant of certiorari as improvidently granted, returning the case to the Ninth Circuit. In March 2025 the Trump administration's DOJ voluntarily dismissed the government's suit against Idaho, nullifying the prior statewide injunction that had required Idaho hospitals to permit EMTALA-based emergency abortions notwithstanding Idaho's near-total abortion ban.
relevance_note: Leaves most Idaho providers, and by extension providers in other states with strict abortion bans, without a clear federal EMTALA backstop for emergency abortion care; a bellwether for EMTALA/state-abortion-law conflicts nationally.
model_link_note: A dismissed case; no parameter depends on it.

title: St. Luke's Health System v. Labrador - EMTALA Preliminary Injunction (Idaho, Narrow Scope)
summary: Following dissolution of the broader Idaho v. United States injunction, a federal district court in a separate suit preserved an EMTALA-based exception to Idaho's criminal abortion ban, but limited the injunction's scope to St. Luke's Health System hospitals and physicians only. The case remains before Senior Judge B. Lynn Winmill: a September 23, 2026 order extended fact discovery to March 22, 2027 and dispositive motions to May 4, 2027, and the docket shows no appeal.
relevance_note: Illustrates the current provider-by-provider patchwork resolving EMTALA/abortion-ban conflicts rather than a uniform national rule.
model_link_note: A narrow injunction; no parameter depends on it.

title: Public Health Service Act §319 - Public Health Emergency Declaration Authority
summary: Section 319 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. §247d), originally enacted in 1944 and substantially restructured by the Pandemic and All-Hazards Preparedness Act of 2006 (P.L. 109-417), gives the HHS Secretary authority to declare a public health emergency, unlocking emergency funding, liability protections, and related regulatory flexibilities such as FDA Emergency Use Authorization. This standing authority was used for COVID-19, mpox, and other recent declarations and remains in effect independent of PAHPA's currently lapsed programmatic reauthorization.
relevance_note: Foundational baseline authority for any pandemic or emergency-response simulation scenario, distinct from the (currently lapsed) PAHPA program funding.
model_link_note: Standing emergency authority the plan keeps; no parameter prices it.

title: Pandemic and All-Hazards Preparedness Act (PAHPA) - Reauthorization Lapsed, Programs Running on Continuing Resolutions
summary: PAHPA's most recent reauthorization (2019) expired at the end of 2023. Congress has kept most PAHPA programs, including the Hospital Preparedness Program, Strategic National Stockpile authorities, and BARDA, funded only through short-term continuing-resolution extensions rather than a full multi-year reauthorization. Reps. Neal Dunn and Lori Trahan opened a stakeholder request for information on January 27, 2026; an industry letter of September 14, 2026 urging reauthorization reports that no bill had been introduced.
relevance_note: Key structural vulnerability: U.S. pandemic-preparedness infrastructure currently lacks stable multi-year statutory authorization, a material input for emergency-preparedness simulation.
model_link_note: Programs continue on short-term funding; the public-health expansion is priced from readiness gaps, not from this authorization.

title: Conrad State 30 and Physician Access Reauthorization Act (S.709 / H.R.1585) - Program Lapsed Pending Reauthorization
domain_tags: Workforce & Scope of Practice;Rural & Underserved Access
summary: The Conrad 30 program lets each state waive the two-year home-residency requirement for up to 30 J-1 foreign medical graduates per year who commit to three years of service in a Health Professional Shortage Area or Medically Underserved Area. The waiver lapsed for new J-1 entrants as of October 1, 2025 amid a federal government shutdown. S.709/H.R.1585 would reauthorize the program and let high-demand states increase waivers from 30 to up to 35 per year; S.709 had not left the Senate Judiciary Committee as of October 10, 2026 (Congress.gov).
relevance_note: Directly affects the physician pipeline into rural and underserved areas; an unresolved gap worth tracking for workforce-supply modeling.
model_link_note: A pending bill; if enacted it would bear on the workforce pipeline, which the Workforce chapter sizes outside the cost model.

title: CMS Repeal of Nursing Home Minimum Staffing Standards
summary: CMS rescinded the 2024 rule's numerical minimum staffing requirements (0.55 RN and 2.45 nurse-aide hours per resident day, 3.48 total, plus 24/7 onsite RN coverage), citing Congress's postponement of the requirements' implementation to 2035 and a Northern District of Iowa ruling that vacated them as exceeding CMS's statutory authority. Enhanced facility-assessment and Medicaid staffing-spending disclosure requirements from the 2024 rule remain in place.
relevance_note: Reverses the single largest federal nursing-home quality mandate of the past decade; a central input for long-term-care staffing and quality simulation.
model_link_note: Measured: the long-term care parameters are anchored on CBO's comprehensive-LTSS option and a demand-sized workforce, not on a staffing ratio, so the repeal moves no figure (research/long_term_care_methodology.md says so).

title: Rural Health Transformation (RHT) Program (One Big Beautiful Bill Act)
summary: Created by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21), RHT provides $50 billion over five years, $10 billion per year from 2026 through 2030, to states for rural health system strengthening. Half of each year's funding is distributed equally across all approved states; half is awarded competitively based on rurality metrics, existing rural health system conditions, and proposed state initiatives. CMS announced first-year awards to all 50 states in early 2026, averaging roughly $200 million per state.
relevance_note: Largest-ever dedicated federal rural health funding stream; a major offsetting input against OBBBA's Medicaid cuts to rural providers, and central to rural-hospital-solvency modeling.
model_link_note: Adds federal rural health funding for 2026 to 2030, which the June 2025 baseline projections predate, as they predate the rest of the law; it ends before the mature year, so no expansion parameter moves.

title: FTC Vacatur of the 2024 Noncompete Ban Rule
domain_tags: Market Structure & Antitrust;Workforce & Scope of Practice
summary: The FTC voted 3-1 on September 5, 2025 to vacate its own 2024 rule that would have banned most employer noncompete agreements nationwide, including in healthcare. The Commission signaled it will instead pursue noncompetes case-by-case under traditional antitrust and unfair-competition enforcement, and on September 10, 2025 sent letters to large healthcare employers urging review of existing noncompete agreements.
relevance_note: Directly affects physician and clinician labor-market mobility assumptions, especially in hospital-system and staffing-agency consolidation scenarios.
model_link_note: The 2024 ban never took effect: a court set it aside nationwide in August 2024, before its effective date. Its vacatur leaves the status quo the workforce figures were built on unchanged.

title: FTC Final Rule - Hart-Scott-Rodino Premerger Notification Overhaul
summary: Published November 12, 2024 and effective February 10, 2025, this is the most sweeping revision to HSR premerger notification filing requirements in decades. It requires substantially more transaction detail, including separate forms for acquiring and acquired parties, and was explicitly framed by then-Chair Lina Khan as targeting private-equity roll-up strategies in industries including healthcare.
relevance_note: Increases pre-closing disclosure burden and antitrust-review lead time for hospital, physician-group, and other healthcare consolidation deals; relevant to market-structure simulation.
model_link_note: A merger-filing rule; no parameter depends on it.

title: Senator Elizabeth Dole 21st Century Veterans Healthcare and Benefits Improvement Act - Community Care Referral Streamlining
summary: Signed January 2, 2025 (H.R.8371, 118th Congress), described as the largest expansion of VA services since the PACT Act, with provisions spanning health care, caregiver support, and other veterans' benefits. Among its health care provisions, VA implemented streamlined "best medical interest" community-care referral determinations as of May 2025, removing a secondary review step and giving veterans faster access to non-VA MISSION Act community care.
relevance_note: Speeds veteran access to community care, a channel that now delivers roughly 40% of all VA-funded health care.
model_link_note: Changes VA community-care referral inside the status quo; no parameter moves.

title: FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (P.L. 119-60) - Tricare Provisions
summary: Signed December 18, 2025. Section 701 cuts the distance that triggers the Tricare Prime Travel Benefit (reimbursement for specialty-care travel costs) from 100 to 75 miles for active-duty members and their dependents; the section names no later date, so it took effect December 18, 2025, and TRICARE's travel-benefit page applies it. Section 713 extends the limit on cutting military medical end strength from five years to ten, and section 714 requires Joint Chiefs and Surgeon General endorsements before a military treatment facility's services are modified. The act also directs increased cross-credentialing of VA and military-treatment-facility providers. The final act dropped the IVF expansion both chambers had passed, so TRICARE still covers assisted reproduction only for service-connected infertility.
relevance_note: Directly affects access-to-specialty-care and benefit-scope assumptions for the roughly 9.6 million Tricare beneficiaries.
model_link_note: TRICARE access provisions inside the status quo; no parameter moves.

title: Trump v. Slaughter - FTC Commissioners' Removal Protection Held Unconstitutional; Humphrey's Executor Overruled (No. 25-332)
summary: Decided June 29, 2026 (6-3). Held that the statute letting the President remove FTC commissioners only for inefficiency, neglect of duty or malfeasance violates the separation of powers, and overruled Humphrey's Executor v. United States (1935): "If anything more is left of Humphrey's, we overrule it." The opinion states that those within the President's general administrative control must be removable at will, and leaves tenure protection for non-Article III courts undecided. The Court decided only the FTC's protection. In Trump v. Cook the same day, it denied the President's application to remove a Federal Reserve governor while her challenge proceeds, and the majority described that ruling as upholding the Federal Reserve as currently structured; CRS (LSB11448) reads similar protections at other multimember agencies as on precarious footing.
relevance_note: Removes the premise that an executive regulator can be insulated from presidential removal. The Legislation, Governance and Executive Hardening chapters state the holding in one shared sentence, and the plan's hardening relies instead on statutory duties, mandatory funding, defaults, courts and legislative offices.
model_link_note: Constrains the governance design, not a cost; the governance parameter prices bodies, not their tenure.

title: Moore v. United States - Mandatory Repatriation Tax Upheld; Taxes on Wealth Left Undecided (No. 22-800)
summary: Decided June 20, 2024 (7-2). Upheld the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act's one-time Mandatory Repatriation Tax, which taxes American shareholders on the realized but undistributed income of foreign corporations they control. The Court stated that its analysis does not address taxes on holdings, wealth or net worth, or taxes on appreciation, so whether an annual wealth tax must be apportioned among the states remains undecided.
relevance_note: The plan's financing package includes a wealth tax whose constitutionality rests on the question this decision expressly left open; the Tax chapter says so.
model_link_note: Leaves open whether a wealth tax must be apportioned among the states, a legal risk to the yield the parameter assumes.

title: Trump v. Cook - Federal Reserve Governor Kept in Office Pending Litigation (No. 25A312)
summary: Decided June 29, 2026 (5-4), the same day as Trump v. Slaughter, after argument on the President's application to stay a lower-court order keeping Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook in office. The Court denied the application on the narrow ground that the President had not given her the notice and opportunity to respond to which the statute's for-cause protection entitles her, and held that "cause" sets a substantial threshold without defining it. The government did not contest the protection's constitutionality; the majority, answering a dissent that called it unconstitutional, described its ruling as upholding the Federal Reserve as currently structured. The case continues in the lower courts.
relevance_note: Marks the edge of Trump v. Slaughter: on the same day the Court treated the Federal Reserve governors' protection differently from the FTC's. The crosswalk cites it to explain why the dashboard reads Slaughter as it does.
model_link_note: Bears on how far the removal ruling reaches, not on any cost; the governance parameter prices bodies, not their tenure.

title: Transparency in Coverage Final Rule (CMS-9882-F) - Machine-Readable File Revisions
summary: Published October 6, 2026 (91 FR 63748) by Treasury, Labor and HHS; the rule takes effect December 7, 2026. Its machine-readable file changes apply beginning March 6, 2027 (some provisions September 6, 2027, and the new Utilization File is first posted July 1, 2028), and its consumer-tool section applies for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2027. For the in-network and out-of-network files it adds contextual files and data elements, lengthens the reporting period and lowers the claims threshold for out-of-network data, and reduces the reporting cadence; it requires a text file and footer that make every file findable, including the prescription drug file, and adds phone access to the consumer price tool. On the prescription drug file, the Departments say they plan to begin working to implement it in short order.
relevance_note: Finalizes the December 2025 proposal the 2020 Transparency in Coverage row anticipated; the payer-side price data the plan's public reporting would replace.
model_link_note: A disclosure rule for private plans; no parameter depends on it.

title: 340B Rebate Model Pilot Program - Revised Notice (HRSA)
summary: Published August 3, 2026, after the original pilot was vacated in American Hospital Association v. Kennedy.
